extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical geometry / mathematicians studying Archimedes
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Archimedes' propositions about the geometry of the spiral (ratios, tangents, areas, inscribed/circumscribed sector constructions) and Book I of On the Equilibrium of Planes (postulates and propositions about centres of gravity and balancing weights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 15 (spiral distance ratio with first circle circumference)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P, Q be points on the second turn of the spiral, and OP, OQ meet the ‘first circle’ AKP’Q’ in P’, Q’, and if c be the circumference of the first circle, then OP : OQ = c + (arc AKP’) : c + (arc AKQ’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained by tracking how the moving point on OA describes OP while A describes the whole circumference plus the backward arc AKP'; corollary: for P,Q on the nth turn replace c by (n−1)c so OP:OQ = (n−1)c + (arc AKP') : (n−1)c + (arc AKQ').

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary to Prop. 15 (nth-turn generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P, Q are on the nth turn of the spiral, OP : OQ = (n—1)c + (arc AKP’) : (n—1)c + (arc AKQ’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct consequence of the same counting of full circumferences contributed by earlier turns; used repeatedly in later tangent/angle arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 16–17 (tangent angle signs at any spiral point)
rubrics_metrics.description: If BC be the tangent at P, any point on the spiral, PC being the ‘forward’ part of BC, and if OP be joined, the angle OPC is obtuse while the angle OPB is acute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: compare tangent with circle centered at O with radius OP — the tangent cannot make OPC acute (would be less than right angle to circle tangent) and cannot be right (leads to contradiction via auxiliary construction and area/arc comparisons). Same reasoning extends to nth turns with added full circumferences/arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment for nth turn in tangent proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When P is on the second or nth turn, arcs in the proportion arguments are augmented by p or (n—1)p, where p is the perimeter of the circle through P, and similarly (n—1)c is added to arcs AKR', AKP' where c is circumference of first circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction on how to modify the arc/ perimeter terms in the arguments of Props. 16–17 to account for additional full turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 18–19 (perpendicular to initial line meets tangent at length equal to circle circumference)
rubrics_metrics.description: I. If OA be the initial line, A the end of the first turn, and the tangent to the spiral at A be drawn, the straight line OB drawn from O perpendicular to OA will meet the said tangent in some point B, and OB will be equal to the circumference of the ‘first circle’. II. If A' be the end of the second turn, OB' meets tangent at A' in B' and OB' = 2 (circumference of second circle). III. Generally, if An be the end of the nth turn, and OB meet the tangent at An in Bn, then OBn = n c_n, where c_n is circumference of the nth circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume OB greater or less than the circumference and derive impossibilities using auxiliary lines that meet circle and spiral, comparing arcs and lengths via earlier propositions (Prop. 7, 8, 14, 15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 20 (perpendicular from O to OP meets tangent at length equal to corresponding forward arc)
rubrics_metrics.description: I. If P be any point on the first turn and OT be drawn perpendicular to OP, OT will meet the tangent at P in some point T; and if the circle drawn with centre O and radius OP meet the initial line in K, then OT is equal to the arc of this circle between K and P measured in the ‘forward’ direction of the spiral. II. Generally, if P be on the nth turn, OT = (n—1)p + arc KP (measured ‘forward’), where p is circumference of circle with radius OP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by assuming OT greater or less than the arc and using auxiliary constructions intersecting circle and tangent, then comparing ratios via Prop. 7 and Prop. 14 leading to contradictions. Shows close geometric relation between perpendicular segment and arc-length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 21–23 (approximation by similar circular sectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an area bounded by any arc of a spiral and the lines joining the extremities of the arc to the origin, it is possible to circumscribe about the area one figure, and to inscribe in it another figure, each consisting of similar sectors of circles, and such that the circumscribed figure exceeds the inscribed by less than any assigned area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: bisect the angle BOC repeatedly to produce arbitrarily small sector OCr; construct circumscribed and inscribed figures made of similar sectors with successive radii meeting the spiral. The difference between circumscribed and inscribed reduces to the small sector OCr, which can be made < any given ε; corollary gives ability to approximate the spiral area arbitrarily closely from inside and outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary (approximation conclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) a figure can be circumscribed to the area such that it exceeds the area by less than any assigned space; (2) a figure can be inscribed such that the area exceeds it by less than any assigned space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct consequence of the circumscription/inscription construction in Props. 21–23, important for area computations by limiting processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 24 (area of first turn equals one-third of first circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area bounded by the first turn of the spiral and the initial line is equal to one-third of the ‘first circle’. More generally, if OP be any radius vector in the first turn, the area of the portion of the spiral bounded thereby is equal to one-third of that sector of the circle drawn with radius OP which is bounded by the initial line and OP (measured ‘forward’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using circumscribed and inscribed figures made of similar sectors and comparing sums of sector areas; shows R1 = (1/3) C1. Also indicates how to generalize to portions cut by an arbitrary radius vector and to later turns (with added multiples of full circle areas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization of area described by radius vector up to nth turn
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is on the second or nth turn, the complete area described by the radius vector from the beginning up to position OP is 1/3 (n + 2) times the circle with radius OP, or more generally 1/3 (n+2)(circle with radius), and related expressions when accounting for sectors and rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes explains how areas accumulate across turns and how the radius-vector sweeps areas multiple times; use of proportionality of circle areas to squared radii and previous propositions yields the general expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 25 (second-turn area ratio 7:12)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A1 be the end of the second turn, the area bounded by the second turn and OA1 is to the area of the ‘second circle’ in the ratio of 7 to 12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special case of Prop. 26 where the sector becomes the full second circle (radius doubled): applied by substituting radii relations r2 = 2 r1 to get (R1 + R2) : (second circle) = 7:12, yielding R2 in terms of R1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 26 (general formula for area between two radii along a turn)
rubrics_metrics.description: If BC be any arc measured in the ‘forward’ direction on any turn of a spiral, not being greater than the complete turn, and if a circle be drawn with O as centre and OC as radius meeting OB in B’, then (area of spiral between OB, OC) : (sector OB’C) = {OC·OB + 4(OC − OB)^2} : OC^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by contradiction using circumscribed/inscribed sector-figures; reduces comparison to sums of squares of radii and uses proportionality of similar sectors to squared radii. Provides a closed-form relation for the spiral area between two radii in terms of OB and OC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 27 (areas of rings proportional to successive integers)
rubrics_metrics.description: If R1 denote the area of the first turn bounded by the initial line, R2 the area of the ring added by the second complete turn, R3 that of the ring added by the third turn, and so on, then R2 = 2 R1, R3 = 3 R1, ... generally the ring areas are in the ratio of successive integers 1,2,3,... (i.e., Rk ∝ k−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes derives recurrence relations by comparing sums of ring areas to circle areas (which scale as squares of radii) and uses algebraic manipulations (dirimendo) to show the proportionality of Ri to index; useful for building total-area formulas across turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 28 (ratio of two complementary spiral strip areas E:F)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given BC an arc on a turn, draw circles with centre O radius OB (meeting OC in C') and radius OC (meeting OB produced in B'). Let E be area bounded by larger arc B'C, line B'B and spiral BC; F be area bounded by smaller arc BC', line CC' and spiral BC. Then E : F = {OB + 2(OC − OB)} : {OB + 4(OC − OB)} (equivalently expressed by algebraic manipulation in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Prop. 26 and algebraic combination of proportions between sector areas and constructed quantities; shows how splitting spiral bounded regions relates to simple algebraic functions of OB and OC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 1 (equilibrium principle for equal weights at equal distances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal weights at equal distances are in equilibrium, and equal weights at unequal distances are not in equilibrium but incline towards the weight which is at the greater distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational axiom for the equilibrium theory; used repeatedly to reason about balance and to derive centre-of-gravity relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 2 (effect of adding to a weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, when weights at certain distances are in equilibrium, something be added to one of the weights, they are not in equilibrium but incline towards that weight to which the addition was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A basic monotonicity postulate: increasing a weight tilts the balance toward it; used in reductio arguments about equality and inequalities of weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 3 (effect of removing from a weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarly, if anything be taken away from one of the weights, they are not in equilibrium but incline towards the weight from which nothing was taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement of Postulate 2; used to argue by removing differences to reach equal-weight cases and deduce inequalities of distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 4 (centres coincide for equal similar figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: When equal and similar plane figures coincide if applied to one another, their centres of gravity similarly coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric symmetry principle: when figures are equal and similarly placed, centres coincide — used to transfer centre-of-gravity conclusions between congruent/similar pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 5 (centres correspond in unequal similar figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: In figures which are unequal but similar the centres of gravity will be similarly situated. By points similarly situated in relation to similar figures I mean points such that, if straight lines be drawn from them to the equal angles, they make equal angles with the corresponding sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows mapping of centre-of-gravity locations via similarity; frequently used for scaling arguments and to transfer centroid positions between similar shapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 6 (transfer of equilibrium under equality of magnitudes)
rubrics_metrics.description: If magnitudes at certain distances be in equilibrium, (other) magnitudes equal to them will also be in equilibrium at the same distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits replacement of magnitudes by equal ones without changing equilibrium; used in discrete decomposition arguments (partitioning into equal parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 7 (position of centre for figures with concave perimeter)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any figure whose perimeter is concave in (one and) the same direction the centre of gravity must be within the figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A geometric localization postulate ensuring centroid lies inside simple convex-like figures; used as a constraint in contradiction proofs about centroid placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1 (equal-distance equilibrium implies equal weights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weights which balance at equal distances are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from Postulate 3 by reductio: if unequal, removing the difference contradicts equilibrium — basic logical consequence used to deduce equality from symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2 (unequal weights at equal distances incline to greater)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unequal weights at equal distances will not balance but will incline towards the greater weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from removing the difference and applying Postulates 1–2; establishes monotonic tilt behavior for unequal weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3 (unequal weights balance at unequal distances reciprocally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unequal weights will balance at unequal distances, the greater weight being at the lesser distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive argument showing if A and B balance about C then AC < BC (greater weight closer); converse also given. Uses reductio and Postulates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 4 (centre of gravity of two equal weights)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two equal weights have not the same centre of gravity, the centre of gravity of both taken together is at the middle point of the line joining their centres of gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by reduction to Prop. 3 and appeals to previously established lever relations (reference to lost 'On levers'); gives rule for combining equal masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 5 (centre of gravity of three equal magnitudes in line)
rubrics_metrics.description: If three equal magnitudes have their centres of gravity on a straight line at equal distances, the centre of gravity of the system will coincide with that of the middle magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate corollary of Prop. 4; extended in corollaries to odd/even numbers of equal parts arranged symmetrically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 6–7 (two magnitudes balance at distances reciprocally proportional to magnitudes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two magnitudes, whether commensurable (Prop. 6) or incommensurable (Prop. 7), balance at distances reciprocally proportional to the magnitudes. Given A:B = DC:CE, placing A at C and B at D balances about the division C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prop. 6 gives a discrete constructive proof using common measures and partition into equal parts; Prop. 7 handles incommensurable case via approximation and reducing to commensurable remainders. Fundamental lever law in Archimedes' framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 8 (centre of gravity of remainder after removing part)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AB be a magnitude whose centre of gravity is C, and AD a part of it whose centre of gravity is F, then the centre of gravity of the remaining part will be a point G on FC produced such that GC : CF = (AD) : (DE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit ratio locating the centroid of the remainder after removing a subpart; used in composite-centroid calculations and proofs by partitioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 9 (parallelogram centroid lies on line joining midpoints of opposite sides)
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of any parallelogram lies on the straight line joining the middle points of opposite sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by partitioning into many equal parallelograms and using symmetry (Postulate 4) and previous propositions about equal parts; precursor to Prop. 10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10 (parallelogram centroid is intersection of diagonals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of a parallelogram is the point of intersection of its diagonals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of Prop. 9: the bisectors coincide at the diagonals' intersection; alternative proof via applying equal triangles to each other (Postulate 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 11 (centroid correspondence under similarity of triangles)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the triangles abc, ABC be similar, and g, G two points in them similarly situated, then if g be the centre of gravity of triangle abc, G must be the centre of gravity of triangle ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses reductio ad absurdum: similarity maps centroid positions; enables transferring centroid conclusions across scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 12 (midpoint/centroid correspondence under similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two similar triangles abc, ABC, and d, D the middle points of bc, BC respectively, then, if the centre of gravity of abc lie on ad, that of ABC will lie on AD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive similarity argument: choose corresponding points and show proportional segments lead to similar situated centres; supports scaling of centroid lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 13 (centroid lies on median in triangle)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any triangle the centre of gravity lies on the straight line joining any angle to the middle point of the opposite side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by subdividing triangle into many small parallelograms and triangles and using Prop. 9 and Prop. 8 to eliminate possibilities; alternative proof via similarity and centroid of subtriangles. Establishes that centroid lies on each median.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 14 (centroid at intersection of two medians)
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of any triangle is at the intersection of the lines drawn from any two angles to the middle points of the opposite sides respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate corollary of Prop. 13; gives classical result that centroid is intersection of medians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 15 (centroid location for a trapezium formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AD, BC be the two parallel sides of a trapezium ABCD, AD being the smaller, and if AD, BC be bisected at E, F respectively, then the centre of gravity of the trapezium is at a point G on EF such that GE : GF = (2·BC + AD) : (2·AD + BC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces trapezium to combination of triangles with known centroids by extending BA, CD to meet at O and using decomposition and proportional division of diagonal BD into three equal parts to identify centroid via symmetry arguments and previous propositions.
